name: Automata & Pre-History
summary: Centuries of mechanical figures built to imitate the human body before electronics or feedback control existed. From Leonardo's cable-driven knight and Vaucanson's musicians to Westinghouse's showroom robots, these machines ran on clockwork, hydraulics, and gramophone records. They established the cultural idea of an artificial human and worked out early mechanisms for jointed limbs, but none could sense their surroundings or keep their own balance.
themes: the cultural idea of an artificial human

name: Foundational Research
summary: Universities and labs began treating the humanoid as an engineering problem. Waseda University's WABOT-1 (1973) was the first full-scale anthropomorphic robot to combine limbs, vision, tactile hands, and speech; WABOT-2 played the organ. Work in this era was slow and quasi-static — robots shifted weight carefully and paused between steps — but it produced the first real theories of bipedal balance and limb coordination.
themes: the humanoid as an engineering problem

name: Dynamic Bipedalism
summary: Two threads ran in parallel. In Marc Raibert's Leg Laboratory — Carnegie Mellon from 1980, MIT from 1987 — machines learned to balance before they learned to walk: a one-legged hopper, then in 1985 the Planar Biped, the first robot to run on two legs, doing flips by 1986 and somersaults in 3D by 1992. Meanwhile Honda spent a secret decade on the E- and P-series, culminating in P2 (1996) and ASIMO (2000): battery-powered humanoids that walked, and eventually ran, under predictive control. Sony's QRIO, AIST's HRP line, KAIST's HUBO and Waseda's WABIAN followed, alongside child-sized platforms like iCub, NAO and the Kondo hobby kits, and Hiroshi Ishiguro's uncanny androids. Locomotion moved from a curiosity to something demonstrably solvable.

name: DARPA Robotics Challenge Era
summary: Prompted by the Fukushima disaster, DARPA funded a competition for humanoids that could drive, walk over rubble, open doors, and use power tools in a degraded environment. Boston Dynamics' hydraulic Atlas, NASA's electric Valkyrie, and KAIST's DRC-HUBO+ (the 2015 winner) pushed whole-body manipulation and rough-terrain locomotion hard — and made the gap between lab demos and real-world reliability very public.

name: Commercial Pivot
summary: The question shifted from 'can it walk?' to 'what is it for?'. Agility Robotics turned the Cassie legs into Digit, a bipedal robot aimed at warehouse logistics; SoftBank shipped tens of thousands of the wheeled social robot Pepper; Engineered Arts sold expressive androids to museums. Tesla's 2021 announcement of Optimus signaled that a much larger wave was coming.

name: The Explosion
summary: Cheap high-torque electric actuators, cheap compute, and — decisively — vision-language-action models converged. Dozens of well-funded general-purpose humanoids appeared almost at once: Tesla Optimus, Figure 01/02/03, 1X NEO, Unitree H1/G1, Apptronik Apollo, Sanctuary Phoenix, Fourier GR-series, plus a large Chinese cohort (XPeng, AgiBot, Booster, Unitree). Locomotion is largely a solved commodity; the open problems are dexterous manipulation, autonomy, reliability, and cost.
themes: manipulation and autonomy as the frontier
